title: British Airways Must Pay Rs 1.05 Lakh After Turning Away Green Card Holder
excerpt: A Hyderabad consumer commission found deficiency in service and unfair trade practice in the April 2023 denial, ordering Rs 50,000 compensation, Rs 50,000 in punitive damages and Rs 5,000 in costs, payable within 45 days.
body:
• A Hyderabad consumer commission has ordered British Airways to pay Rs 1.05 lakh after it denied boarding to a 78-year-old US green card holder at Hyderabad airport and had him escorted out.
  • Dr Kattar Divaker Rao's passport and green card were checked before his ticket was issued, and he reconfirmed his journey 72 hours before his April 25, 2023 flight to Chicago via London.
  • The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-II, Hyderabad, held in its November 3, 2026 order that stopping him at the last moment over a UK transit visa was a deficiency in service and an unfair trade practice.
  • For green card holders: an airline checking your documents at booking is not a guarantee at the gate — verify the transit-visa rules for every connection yourself before you travel.

British Airways has been ordered to pay Rs 1.05 lakh for refusing to let a 78-year-old US green card holder board his flight from Hyderabad to Chicago and having him escorted out of the airport. In an order dated November 3, 2026, the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-II, Hyderabad, found the airline guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, according to The Times of India.

What happened at Hyderabad airport

Dr Kattar Divaker Rao, a medical doctor and a permanent resident of the United States since 1981, had booked a British Airways ticket to travel on April 25, 2023, from Hyderabad to Chicago via London, transiting at Heathrow Airport. The Times of India reports that the ticket was issued nearly two months before the journey, after the airline had checked his passport and valid US green card; The Indian Express reports he booked on February 16 and had made more than 40 journeys between India and the US. He reconfirmed his journey 72 hours before departure.

On the day of travel, the airline refused to let him board, saying he did not have a UK transit visa. A woman officer escorted him and his luggage towards the airport exit, and he was not allowed to approach the airport authorities to resolve the issue, both reports say. He returned home and travelled to the United States two days later by another airline.

"The all of sudden obstruction just before the boarding of the flight caused by the Opposite Party.No.1, even though the Complainant holding a Green card after confirming the ticket to travel is nothing but unfair coupled with deficiency in the services rendered towards the Complainant."

— District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-II, Hyderabad, as reported by The Times of India

The airline's defence

British Airways argued, as recorded in the order, that a UK transit visa was mandatory for changing flights at Heathrow, that Dr Rao had not produced any document showing he was exempt, and that it had refunded Rs 1,48,834 to the travel agent. The Indian Express adds that the airline argued his US-issued Alien Card, issued before April 1, 1998, did not qualify. The commission questioned why the airline had issued and reconfirmed the ticket if it objected to his documents. The travel agent did not file its written version within the stipulated period, and GMR, the airport operator, said decisions on whether a passenger could travel rested solely with the airline.

The order

The bench — president Vakkanti Narasimha Rao and members P V T R Jawahar Babu and Suma Vala — partly allowed the complaint, which The Indian Express reports was first filed before the Ranga Reddy District Consumer Commission on April 23, 2025, and later transferred to Hyderabad. It held that Dr Rao had faced harassment and humiliation, directed the airline to discontinue the unfair practice, and gave it 45 days from receiving the order to comply. The claims against the travel agent and GMR were dismissed, and Dr Rao's remaining claims, including a demand for Rs 10 lakh in damages and Rs 1.7 lakh towards the ticket value, were disallowed.

What this means for green card holders

The ruling turns on sequence: the documents were examined before the ticket was sold, the journey was reconfirmed, and the objection came only at the airport. Travellers connecting through a third country should still verify the transit rules for their exact documents on every leg — including older green cards — rather than relying on the booking check alone, and should ask for a denial reason in writing at the counter. In India, consumer complaints of this kind can be raised through the National Consumer Helpline, 1915, as noted in The Indian Express report.
